title: Building a New Community
subtitle: The Prophet's Mosque, the Assembly of Faith, and the Bench of the Suffah
summary: Purchasing the land from the two orphans, the Prophet working with bare hands alongside his companions to construct Al-Masjid al-Nabawi, the multifunctional heart of the new society, the academic sanctuary of Ahl al-Suffah, and the institutional foundations of Madinan civic life.

sections.text: The Purchase of the Sacred Ground

Upon settling in the home of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, the Prophet's immediate priority was the establishment of a communal center for worship, education, and social leadership. The plot where his camel Al-Qaswa had knelt was a palm-drying yard belonging to two orphan boys, Sahl and Suhayl, under the guardianship of As'ad ibn Zurarah. The young boys stepped forward generously and offered the land as a gift for God and His Messenger.

The Prophet ﷺ, however, insisted on strict justice and commercial ethics. Refusing to take the land without fair compensation from two vulnerable orphans, he negotiated its fair market value of ten gold dinars and purchased the plot, funded through Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. The ground was cleared of graves of pre-Islamic pagan antiquity, dilapidated palm stumps were leveled, and the muddy ground was prepared for construction.
The humble desert environment where the foundations of the Prophet's Mosque were laid.
Erecting the Prophet's Mosque with Bare Hands

The construction of Al-Masjid al-Nabawi was an exercise in shared labor, humility, and spiritual camaraderie. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ did not merely supervise; he rolled up his sleeves, carried sun-dried adobe mud bricks and heavy foundation stones upon his own shoulders, and labored side by side with the Muhajirun and Ansar.

Seeing the Messenger of God carrying stones, companions pleaded with him: 'O Messenger of God, let us carry them for you!' But the Prophet insisted on sharing their toil, chanting rhythmic verses of encouragement along with them:

اللَّهُمَّ لَا عَيْشَ إِلَّا عَيْشُ الْآخِرَهْ * فَاغْفِرْ لِلْأَنْصَارِ وَالْمُهَاجِرَهْ
'O God! There is no true life except the life of the Hereafter, so grant forgiveness to the Ansar and the Muhajirah!' (Sahih al-Bukhari)

The original building was a model of austere functionality. Its foundations were stone, its walls unbaked mud brick, its pillars felled trunks of date palms, and its roof thatched palm fronds plastered with clay. The floor remained bare sand and pebbles; when heavy rains fell, mud covered the floor where the worshippers bowed in prayer. Adjoining the eastern wall of the mosque were constructed modest private living quarters (Hujurat) of mud and palm thatch for the Prophet's household.
The Multifunctional Heart of the Community

The mosque was the place of the five prayers, of hearing the Quran, and of the Prophet's consultation with his companions. People brought their questions there. Guests were received, and the poor who had no house were given the shaded end of the court, the Suffah. It was not a court with a later constitution, and it was not a clinic. When someone was hurt, care was the care people give in a community that gathers in one place. The building's work, as the reports describe it, was worship, teaching, counsel, and hospitality.

In the rows of prayer a man of Quraysh, a man of the Ansar, and a former slave stood in whatever place the row left open. The mosque did not erase every tie of kinship outside the prayer. It did put them, for the prayer, on one line, facing one direction, which in those first months was still Jerusalem.
The quiet courtyards of learning and devotion where the companions gathered around the Prophet.
Ahl al-Suffah: The First Residential Academy

At the rear northern end of the mosque, the Prophet erected a shaded, roofed veranda known as Al-Suffah (The Bench). This became a residential hospice and educational academy for destitute emigrants, unmarried companions, and foreign students of faith who possessed neither homes nor wealth in Madinah.

The numbers given for the people of the Suffah vary with the year, from scores to a larger company. They stayed for the prayer, the Quran, and whatever the Prophet taught. Abu Hurayrah became one of the best known of them, but he reached Madinah years later, after Khaybar, and was not among the first residents at the Hijrah. The Prophet shared food that came to him with the people of the Suffah.

From that court of brick and palm the community prayed, learned, and settled the questions of the day. The apartments along the eastern side were the Prophet's household. The Suffah was the lodging of those who had nowhere else to sleep.
